summary: SQLite WAL checkpointing copies committed content from the -wal file into the main database file. Auto-checkpoints run at 1000 pages in PASSIVE mode. FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE wait for readers and writers and add guarantees. An active reader pins the WAL: a checkpoint cannot copy past its end mark, so overlapping readers starve checkpoints and the WAL grows without bound. Tuning uses wal_autocheckpoint, the wal_checkpoint pragma, and the pnLog/pnCkpt counters. The 2026 WAL-reset bug, fixed in 3.51.3, can corrupt databases when a checkpoint and a write race across connections. SQLite and Canonical both call real-world impact very low.

claims.text: A checkpoint copies committed content from the WAL file back into the database file. The writer rewinds the WAL to its start only after the whole WAL is copied and synced and no reader still uses it.

By default SQLite auto-checkpoints on the COMMIT that makes the WAL 1000 pages or more (about 4 MB). It also checkpoints when the last connection to the database closes. The SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT compile-time option changes that default.
Automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE. sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() is also PASSIVE, and PASSIVE is the default checkpoint style.
PASSIVE copies as many frames as it can without waiting for readers or writers. It can leave the checkpoint unfinished. It never invokes the busy handler.

FULL waits, invoking the busy handler, until no writer is active and all readers use the most recent snapshot. It then copies all frames and syncs the database file. While it is pending it blocks new writers, but not new readers.
RESTART does what FULL does. It then waits, invoking the busy handler, until all readers use only the database file. The next writer then restarts the WAL from its beginning.
TRUNCATE does what RESTART does. Before a successful return it also truncates the WAL file to zero bytes.
A default checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file. SQLite overwrites the WAL from the beginning instead, so the file keeps its high-water size unless journal_size_limit is set.

A checkpoint copies WAL content only up to the end mark of each active reader. It stops at the first WAL page past any active reader's end mark, remembers how far it got, and resumes on a later call. A long read transaction therefore prevents checkpoint progress.
Checkpoints are mutually exclusive across processes. If another process is already running a checkpoint, the call fails with SQLITE_BUSY, and the busy handler is not invoked in that case.

A checkpoint syncs in a fixed order. The WAL is synced before its content moves into the database, and the database file is synced before the WAL is reset. PASSIVE syncs the database only when every frame was copied. FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE sync the database after copying all frames.

By default, the thread that makes the COMMIT that crosses the threshold runs that checkpoint itself. That COMMIT is slow while most others stay fast. An app can turn auto-checkpointing off and run checkpoints on its own schedule.

PRAGMA wal_checkpoint and PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(MODE) run a checkpoint on the named database, or on all attached databases if none is named. The no-argument form equals sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(). The argument form equals sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() with that mode.
PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N sets the auto-checkpoint threshold in pages. A value of zero or less turns auto-checkpointing off. The pragma wraps the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface.

sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() writes two counts to its output pointers. pnLog is the total frame count in the WAL. pnCkpt is the number of checkpointed frames, including frames copied by earlier checkpoints. Both are -1 on error or when the database is not in WAL mode. After a successful TRUNCATE both are 0.
PRAGMA journal_size_limit=N makes SQLite truncate a WAL file larger than N bytes back to N, checked at each commit and WAL reset. The default is -1 (no limit). Zero truncates to the minimum size.

SQLite's docs suggest turning off automatic checkpoints and running checkpoints during idle moments or in a separate thread or process. Syncthing runs a timer-based checkpointer but leaves auto-checkpoints on, and its authors say the two contend.

For a WAL that keeps growing under overlapping readers, the docs suggest reader gaps, or manual RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints that run to completion. Litestream's guide says to shorten long read transactions.

Litestream's default schedule: a PASSIVE checkpoint when the WAL passes 1,000 pages (about 4 MB), or one minute after the last attempt if the WAL has at least 1 page. A forced TRUNCATE is considered only at 121,359 pages (about 500 MB), and only after a passive restart fails to bring the WAL back under that limit.

Checkpoint frequency trades read speed against write speed. Frequent checkpoints keep the WAL small and reads fast. Rare checkpoints spread the cost over more writes. The SQLite docs say the 1000-page default seems to work well in test applications on workstations, and other strategies may suit other platforms or workloads.
If automatic checkpointing is off and nothing else checkpoints, nothing stops the WAL from growing. Setting wal_autocheckpoint to zero or less turns automatic checkpointing off.

If at least one reader is always active, no checkpoint can complete, and the WAL grows without bound. This is checkpoint starvation. A Syncthing thread posted 2026-02-06 describes the same pattern under near-constant reads and writes.

A forced TRUNCATE waits for all active readers and writers to finish before it truncates the WAL. Litestream says this can block writes and readers for a long time when a long-lived read transaction is open.

FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE hold off new writers while they are pending. On a busy database that stalls commits until the checkpoint returns. Litestream's guide warns that aggressive checkpointing can block writes while read transactions are active.

A very large write transaction makes the WAL large, because the WAL cannot reset while the transaction runs. The docs warn that WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error for transactions over a gigabyte, though they also say that since 3.11.0 WAL handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode.

To tell whether a checkpoint finished, compare the counters. A pnCkpt below pnLog means frames in the WAL were not copied. The first column of the wal_checkpoint pragma is 1 when a RESTART, FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked.

Litestream logs 'passive checkpoint skipped' when a passive checkpoint returns SQLITE_BUSY. It logs 'forcing truncate checkpoint wal_size=... threshold=...' when it forces a blocking TRUNCATE, and 'wal restarted by passive checkpoint, skipping truncate checkpoint wal_size=... threshold=...' when the passive restart avoids one. Only the forcing line marks a blocking checkpoint.

The WAL-reset bug can corrupt a WAL-mode database. SQLite's docs say it is likely present in every release from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) and later. Backports are 3.44.6 and 3.50.7.

The WAL-reset bug needs two or more connections, in separate threads or processes, that write or checkpoint at the same instant. One checkpoint finishes and a second starts. Another connection then commits a WAL reset. A data race hides that reset from the second checkpoint, and a third checkpoint later skips part of the committed transaction.

SQLite says the bug's occurrence rate appears to be at or below the rate of SSD malfunctions or cosmic-ray hits, with no numeric rate given. Canonical's dqlite team says the real-world impact is very low.

SQLite's update dated 2026-08-24 says Phil Eaton devised a reproducer that does not use the sqlite3_test_control() hook. Before that, developers could trigger the bug only by modifying the SQLite sources to call a callback set through sqlite3_test_control().

Canonical's dqlite team built a TLA+ model of the WAL and found a missing-page trace in 20 states. They report that dqlite is not affected, because dqlite blocks user-started checkpoints and disables automatic ones.

disagreements.text: SQLite's wal.html section 6 says RESTART and TRUNCATE can make readers block. The C API and PRAGMA pages say those modes block new writers but do not impede readers. The docs do not reconcile the two.

Litestream says a passive checkpoint returns SQLITE_BUSY when readers or writers are active. The C API page says PASSIVE never waits and never invokes the busy handler, and it ties SQLITE_BUSY to a concurrent checkpoint or to an exhausted busy handler in FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE.
Dates differ. wal.html says the WAL-reset bug was found and fixed on 2026-03-03. Canonical says SQLite disclosed the bug and published the fix on March 5, 2026.

open_questions: Does PASSIVE ever return SQLITE_BUSY? Litestream says yes; the SQLite pages do not say so. A two-connection test would settle it.
Do RESTART and TRUNCATE block readers? See disagreement 1. The docs conflict, and only a test would settle it.
Tailscale's incident count (19 corruption events over about six months, per a secondary summary) was not read from a primary source. Treat it as unverified.
theconsensus.dev's WAL-reset write-up returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch. Its reproducer details (two threads, three connections) come from a search snippet and are unverified.
The Litestream guide has no on-page date. verified_as_of uses its HTTP Last-Modified date, 2026-07-30.
The sqlite.org wal.html footer says 2026-08-25, but its HTTP Last-Modified says 2026-10-13. verified_as_of uses the footer date.
The Syncthing thread has one author and no measurements. Its feedback-loop claim is asserted, not shown.
Canonical's post names no fixed version in its running text. The 3.51.3 fix comes from the SQLite release log.
Which distribution or vendor builds carry the 3.44.6 and 3.50.7 backports? Not checked.
